# Deterministic execution and replay: design and implementation plan

Status: proposal, not implemented. Prepared 2026-09-05 against Mycelium HEAD `c719ad8`. This plan is based on targeted inspection of persistence, clocks, governor decisions and existing test models. No repository code changes or new test runs were performed.

## 1. Architectural decision

Add a deterministic execution environment, provisionally `mycelium-sim`, that runs selected production components against controlled time, randomness, transport, storage and scheduling. Expand coverage incrementally rather than requiring an immediate runtime rewrite.

The design goal is a reproducible explanation of behaviour: given the recorded initial state, build, inputs and execution choices, the same covered code makes the same transitions and reaches the same failure.

Distinguish three modes:

- **Exploration:** a seeded scheduler and fault generator discover executions and save failing histories.
- **Exact replay:** consume recorded environmental choices and check that the same pinned build requests the same effects and produces the same observations. Stop at the first divergence.
- **Scenario replay:** run a causal workload/fault script against changed code. Internal execution may differ; compare contracts and results. This is the mode used to validate a fix or compare governor policies.

A seed is convenient, but not a complete long-lived reproduction artifact. A code change, new random draw, dependency update or different initial disk state can change its execution. Preserve the trace and build manifest as well as the seed.

## 2. Existing foundations

| Current surface | Reuse | Required seam |
|---|---|---|
| `mycelium-core/src/persistence.rs` | WAL encoding/replay, snapshot merge, writer task and regression tests | Storage operations and task scheduling controlled without duplicating persistence logic |
| `mycelium-core/src/ops.rs` | Public operation sequencing around WAL, memory apply and gossip | Stable operation/event identities and explicit observation of each acknowledgement boundary |
| `mycelium-core/src/hlc.rs` | Actual HLC arithmetic, drift handling and ordering | Inject physical clock readings; never replace HLC behaviour with simulator-global time |
| `mycelium-core/src/kv_persist.rs` | Timed advertisement refresh/retraction | Controlled timers, channel readiness and cancellation |
| `src/agent/membership_governor.rs` | Pure `decide`, probabilities and existing cooldowns | Inject random rolls, elapsed time, observations and execution of chosen actions |
| `src/agent/opacity.rs` | Extracted pure opacity transition | Share decision code and inject wall/monotonic time and queue observations |
| Wiki curator/store paths | Reconcile/commit boundary and handover integration points | Explicit pause points and protected-resource transaction adapter |
| `loom-spike/tests/*` | Small concurrency models and deliberately broken witnesses | Keep for memory/interleaving properties; connect each model to the covered production pattern |
| Existing property and integration suites | Generated inputs, real transports/filesystems and end-to-end behaviour | Feed minimized simulation failures into durable regressions; retain adapter conformance tests |

The current WAL/snapshot race is already fixed by merging the WAL tail into the snapshot. Tests include `regression_snapshot_retains_wal_record_acked_before_local_apply` and `regression_writer_threshold_snapshot_right_after_ack_keeps_write`. The new work turns their critical schedule into an explicitly controllable history and explores adjacent failure points.

Existing Loom models explicitly abstract production patterns because the production Tokio/papaya code is not directly instrumented. They are useful but do not establish deterministic execution of the fleet. Likewise, a paused Tokio clock alone does not control wall-clock reads, random choices, OS I/O or multi-thread scheduling.

## 3. Extract the smallest useful execution boundaries

Use shared state machines/algorithms with effect adapters, not simulator-specific implementations of the algorithms under test.

A component consumes an input/completion and emits effect requests. A representative interface is:

```rust
fn step(state: &mut State, event: Event, env: &mut DecisionContext)
    -> Vec<Effect>;
```

Effects include timer registration, channel send, network send, storage read/write/sync/rename/truncate, authority transaction and bounded external work. Completion events return through the same component logic. Production adapters use Tokio and real resources; simulation adapters use an event queue and modeled resources.

This interface is illustrative, not a mandate to rewrite every function into one enormous reducer. Keep ordinary pure functions ordinary. For the WAL writer, an explicit operation state machine can issue asynchronous I/O while retaining the real encoding, merge and error-handling functions. For governors, reuse existing pure decisions and move only the observation and actuation boundaries behind interfaces.

A seam must preserve production ordering. The WAL append acknowledgement and subsequent snapshot are distinct observable actions even when they occur during one task poll; the caller's memory apply is separately schedulable. Do not collapse them into an atomic simulator operation and thereby remove the race under test.

Conversely, do not permit impossible interleavings inside an actually atomic operation. Model atomic regions, channel semantics and locks explicitly. A coverage map declares which races are represented at component boundaries and which remain the responsibility of Loom or real-thread tests.

## 4. Control every covered source of nondeterminism

### Clocks

Expose monotonic elapsed time and wall/physical time as distinct interfaces. Each simulated node has its own wall-clock offset, drift and jump schedule. HLC reads those node-local values and processes actual remote timestamps. Pausing a task does not stop the machine's clock; reboot is a different event with explicit clock/identity/persistent-state handling.

Virtual time advances to the next event when no eligible runnable work remains. Timer ordering and missed-tick policies must match the covered production code. Report zero-time livelock or an unfair schedule rather than endlessly advancing an artificial clock to conceal it.

### Randomness

Use a pinned PRNG algorithm with domain-separated streams for node identity fixtures, component decisions, scheduler choices, workload generation and faults. Record stream identity, semantic call site and draw index. Adding a diagnostic random draw must not perturb membership elections.

Record actual outcomes needed for exact replay. Use deterministic synthetic keys in simulation only; production cryptographic randomness is never seeded by the simulator. External cryptographic/cipher outputs can be replayed as recorded adapter results when internal randomness is outside coverage.

### Scheduling and collections

The simulation kernel runs one selected transition at a time with stable actor/event identifiers. It chooses among eligible events while respecting happens-before edges, FIFO guarantees where applicable, lock ownership and documented select priorities. It must represent send completion separately from receipt and task resumption.

Hash-map iteration can alter action or message order even with seeded election randomness. Audit such iteration in covered paths. Use shared explicit ordering where semantics permit it, or model and record the iteration order as an input. Sorting only inside the simulator would test different behaviour. Canonicalize state hashes independently of map layout; do not confuse canonical hashing with deterministic execution.

Exact byte-level reproducibility initially targets a pinned toolchain, dependency lockfile, target and build. Cross-platform semantic replay is a later, separately tested promise, especially for floating-point thresholds and third-party serialization.

### Network

Model node/link/process identity, connection generations, bounded send/receive queues, latency, loss, disconnect and reconnect. For TCP-like streams, preserve in-connection byte order; do not inject arbitrary packet reordering above an ordered stream. Retry/reconnect may produce duplicate application requests, which retain logical operation identity. Model datagram paths separately.

Partitions can be asymmetric and independently affect mesh traffic, authority access and artifact access. Delayed messages from an old process incarnation follow the actual transport/session acceptance rules. A global oracle may inspect all state; controllers cannot.

### External work

Model installation, probes and reconciliation as requested effects with latency, result, resource cost and cancellation behaviour. A paused holder can still have remote I/O complete. Cancelling a task does not automatically undo an external effect.

Recorded LLM output can reproduce downstream decisions without making the model itself deterministic. Label that as boundary replay. DNS, process execution, SQLite internals, TLS and unwrapped dependencies are likewise explicit exclusions until adapted.

## 5. Storage model: persistence means more than a map

Provide a filesystem adapter covering the actual operations used by WAL/snapshot code. Maintain volatile file contents, durable contents, open handles and directory entries separately. Represent write completion, short writes, flush, data synchronization, rename and directory synchronization with distinct effects.

A successful sync establishes only the selected storage profile's guarantee. Unsynced writes may survive or disappear according to recorded crash choices; synchronized data must not disappear in a profile that promises it survives the injected failure. Separate process death, machine power loss, device failure and deliberate data corruption. Do not conflate them into one `crash()` that arbitrarily loses any data.

Use named, versioned storage profiles. A profile with durable atomic rename differs from one requiring parent-directory synchronization after rename. The inspected snapshot path syncs the temporary file, renames it, then truncates and syncs the WAL; the model must not silently insert a directory-sync guarantee. The WAL read-back also currently maps read errors to empty bytes; schedule this failure explicitly to test whether truncation remains safe. These are targets for investigation, not newly validated failure reports.

Crash stops process tasks without executing graceful shutdown, RAII cleanup or a final snapshot. Keep the modeled surviving storage, discard volatile process state, and invoke the real recovery decoder into a fresh store. During a pause, retain process state and let other actors advance.

Reuse the production record framing and LWW implementation for recovery. Test truncated tails and corruption under their documented recovery contract; do not demand recovery from arbitrary permanent corruption without redundancy. Oracles must never grant a durability guarantee merely because `write_all` completed.

Modeling a SQLite transaction as atomic can test a curator protocol, but cannot prove SQLite or its filesystem behaviour. Pair that model with the actual mandate transaction handler on a real SQLite backend and crash-boundary tests. Declare the exact code shared and excluded.

## 6. Trace bundle and replay validation

Every reproducible failure produces a self-contained bundle:

```text
manifest.json        build, features, platform, schema/model versions, seeds
scenario.json        workload, topology, fault envelope, assertions
initial-state/       disk images and required input fixtures
choices.trace        scheduling, time, RNG and fault choices
boundary-events      requests/completions, IDs, causality and payload references
checkpoints/         optional component state digests and restart images
failure.json         assertion, first divergent event, relevant history slice
```

The manifest includes Git revision plus any dirty patch hash, Cargo.lock/toolchain identities, model configuration and trace completeness. Initial state includes configured identities and policy revisions. Persist the final failing bundle before declaring capture complete; a truncated trace is explicitly incomplete.

Events include logical operation ID, node incarnation, actor, local sequence, parent cause, virtual time, relevant HLC and effect type. HLC ordering does not substitute for actual recorded causality. Do not use ephemeral memory addresses as identifiers.

Exact replay verifies that each requested effect matches the next recorded effect before supplying its completion. A different payload, missing event or unexpected random draw yields a precise divergence error. Never keep feeding stale recorded answers after the code has diverged.

State digests cover semantically relevant state: memory entries/tombstones, pending messages and timers, persistence state, acknowledged operations, epochs and governor state. Exclude nondeterministic diagnostic fields explicitly. Hashing final output alone is too weak to identify the first divergence.

Use event counts and byte budgets for bounded traces. Keep full failing prefixes/checkpoints needed for reproduction; a rolling ring that has discarded required inputs is an incident diagnostic, not exact replay. Protect captured evidence with access control and encryption; prefer synthetic data for CI. Redacted payloads cannot claim exact reproduction unless replaced by equivalent deterministic fixtures and labelled accordingly.

The proposed CLI is illustrative and does not exist yet:

```text
mycelium-sim explore --scenario wal-snapshot --seed 42
mycelium-sim replay <bundle> --exact
mycelium-sim minimize <bundle>
mycelium-sim run --scenario handover --fault-script <script>
```

## 7. First scenario A: WAL/snapshot race

Use the actual writer and recovery paths through the new adapters. Begin with the current fixed implementation:

1. Create a write to a key absent from the memory snapshot.
2. Append and sync it in the WAL; send the successful WAL acknowledgement.
3. Keep the caller paused before applying the update to memory.
4. Trigger the threshold snapshot. Let it scan memory, merge the WAL, publish the snapshot and truncate the WAL.
5. Resume the caller to apply the update; then kill the process without graceful shutdown.
6. Restart using only the surviving modeled disk and run the production decoder.
7. Assert that the acknowledged record is represented by recovered state, or legitimately superseded under LWW—not lost merely because snapshotting raced local application.

The acknowledgement under test is the WAL-level successful sync receipt. `WalHandle` has distinct fire-and-forget and synchronized paths. The inspected `ops.rs` paths discard append errors; do not infer a strong caller-facing durability guarantee from a boolean result. Add an assertion for a stronger public contract only when that contract is implemented, or record it as a known failing obligation.

Use a test-only mutant that removes the WAL-tail merge. The harness must reliably detect the historical loss under the same causal schedule. Never keep the mutant in the production branch of the algorithm.

Extend the scenario with:

- Crash at every relevant write/sync/rename/truncate/ack boundary.
- Snapshot read failure, full disk, sync failure, writer exit and cancelled acknowledgement receiver.
- A delayed remote record older than the snapshot watermark for a different key.
- Equal-timestamp LWW conflicts and tombstones within their configured retention window.
- Snapshot deferral due to opacity and concurrent incoming writes at legal scheduling boundaries.

Do not cleanly shut down the writer before inspecting recovery: its final snapshot could repair and mask the failure. Do not silently relax an oracle to make a newly exposed durability failure pass; fix the implementation or narrow the documented guarantee explicitly.

## 8. First scenario B: partitioned ownership handover

Use the explicit curator partition contract from the mandate plan. Actors are old holder A, replacement B, submitter P and protected resource R. Keep mesh partitions distinct from R reachability.

1. Establish A at epoch e and commit proposals with decision provenance.
2. Pause A after reconciliation and before resource mutation admission.
3. Partition mesh communication. Allow an authorized replacement command to reach R.
4. Atomically establish B at e+1 and capture its handover checkpoint.
5. Resume A and deliver its old-epoch request, including a variant where A has refreshed its content CAS version.
6. Reject A at the resource; let B recover provenance and re-evaluate durable pending proposals.
7. Reconnect, duplicate and delay messages; no old request or advertisement restores A's authority.

Oracles check the resource's serialization history: no old-epoch mutation after acknowledged handover, no operation applied twice, durable proposals not silently consumed by a rejected holder, and inherited checkpoint completeness for committed data. An old write ordered before activation is legal; an acknowledgement arriving after handover does not change that order.

Also replay revocation without replacement, authority-service unavailability, lost commit replies, expiry and service restart. Recovery assertions are conditional on restoring the necessary authority/resource connectivity and eligible holder.

The preceding mandate service is a proposal, not assumed shipped. Until its actual commit handler exists, run a clearly labelled contract model plus a legacy wiki characterization scenario. The first handover implementation is complete only when production mandate decisions execute in the harness and a real-backend integration test enforces the same invariant. A toy fence model does not satisfy the delivery gate.

## 9. Extend to interacting governors

Compose demand, provisioning, membership, opacity, retry and snapshot workloads in the same kernel. Reuse the previous stability plan's explicit workload/failure envelope and metrics for overshoot, churn, recovery and work starvation.

Inject workload and local observations rather than giving the controllers a fleet-wide oracle. Represent startup and visibility delays, in-flight capacity, queue service, dropped observation messages and shared resource budgets. Include conflicting intents and timing changes during cooldown.

Compare rule versions using the same offered workload and exogenous fault script. Internal traces may diverge, which is the purpose of the experiment. Keep workload/fault random streams separate from controller draws; record when state-dependent faults prevent a strictly paired comparison.

Check safety continuously and liveness after a declared fault-healing period with fair scheduling. Report offered/admitted/rejected/completed work so rejecting everything cannot win the stability comparison. Treat simulated latency and throughput as properties of a calibrated model, not production benchmarks.

## 10. Oracles, minimization and coverage

Define oracles independently of the transition being tested. Use stable contract IDs linking each assertion to its actual guarantee, observation boundary and environmental assumptions. The durability oracle tracks synced acknowledgements and allowed LWW outcomes; the handover oracle tracks protected-resource order; the governor oracle tracks actual resource occupancy and service progress.

Classify outcomes as safety violation, conditional liveness failure, harness divergence, unsupported environment, or exploration-budget exhaustion. A timed-out exploration is not a proof of deadlock; preserve the runnable set, fairness state and timers for diagnosis.

Minimize failures by removing irrelevant workload operations, nodes, faults and schedule choices while preserving causality and the same contract failure. Do not remove an operation whose completion or persisted bytes another event depends on. Re-run every candidate; minimization itself must be deterministic for a pinned build. Keep the original bundle as evidence and emit a smaller causal scenario for cross-version regression.

Measure reached situations rather than seed counts alone: ack-before-apply snapshots, rename-before-truncate crashes, old-writer arrival after activation, no-heard-peer views, full queues and overlapping controllers. Use deliberately broken witnesses to show each oracle can detect its target failure. Validate scheduler/storage/channel semantics against small known cases before trusting system results.

Keep Loom for fine-grained shared-memory races, property tests for input algebra, real adapter tests for OS/storage/transport contracts, and integration/load tests for actual deployment behaviour. Simulation complements these layers; it does not replace them.

## 11. Implementation sequence and release gates

| PR | Deliverable and exit condition |
|---|---|
| 1 | Nondeterminism inventory, coverage map, oracle contracts, versioned trace schema and the two causal failure scripts |
| 2 | Deterministic event kernel, clock/RNG interfaces and trace record/replay; repeated pinned runs match effect traces and state digests |
| 3 | Storage/channel adapters and WAL writer seams; production semantics preserved by existing regressions and adapter contract tests |
| 4 | WAL/snapshot scenario, fault sweep and mutation witness; failing bundle replays and minimizes without wall-clock sleeps |
| 5 | Partitioned ownership scenario using real mandate code when available; model/production distinction explicit until then |
| 6 | Shared governor adapters, composed workloads, conditional recovery oracles and rule-comparison reports |
| 7 | CI seed corpus, trace retention/security, developer CLI, real-backend checks and contributor guidance |

Deliver PRs 1–4 without waiting for all earlier architecture proposals. PR5 depends on an actual protected-resource authority implementation to meet its full acceptance gate. PR6 consumes the adaptive-control interfaces incrementally. Avoid creating separate simulation harnesses in each companion.

Suggested initial CI policy: small deterministic regressions on every relevant PR, a fixed bounded seed set plus rotating seeds for changed components, and larger scheduled exploration in CI configuration. This plan does not create a scheduled automation. Retain every failing complete bundle and promote minimized novel failures into the regression corpus. Set execution budgets after measuring harness cost; do not substitute a large seed count for meaningful state coverage.

Release requires exact replay to reproduce selected failures, production fixes to pass the corresponding causal scenarios, intentionally broken witnesses to fail, no uncontrolled I/O in declared covered paths, and honest reporting of external dependencies and model assumptions. Static checks can catch forbidden direct clock/RNG/I/O calls in covered modules; an allowlist identifies reviewed production adapters.

## 12. Precedent and practical scope

FoundationDB's paper describes running real database software in deterministic discrete-event simulation with network, disk, time and random-number sources abstracted. It also describes fault injection, workload oracles and limitations arising from dependencies and imperfect operating-system assumptions. The lesson for Mycelium is to share production logic and control its environment—not merely build a separate mathematical model: [FoundationDB paper, section 4](https://www.foundationdb.org/files/fdb-paper.pdf).

Mycelium already has a multi-threaded runtime and concurrency-oriented data structures. Adopt the seam-based approach incrementally, retain its production runtime, and state exactly which execution boundaries are covered. Full instruction-level replay of arbitrary native threads and third-party code is outside the first implementation.

The architectural payoff is a durable artifact for every discovered failure: what happened, which contract failed, the execution choices that made it happen, and a small repeatable test showing whether a change corrects it.
